title: mature for your age
lines: they stole my childhood with a compliment.
at 8, i was handling conversations meant for eighteen.
at 12, i’m solving problems meant for twenty-one.
now i’m an adult who has everything,
but doesn’t know how to enjoy anything.
i deserved to be immature, messy, childish.
i deserved to be a kid.

title: the third parent
lines: not old enough to have authority
but expected to have all the responsibility.
you changed diapers before you could drive.
helped with homework before finishing your own.
made dinner when mom worked late
you raised children before you were done being raised.
now your siblings call you when they need something,
because to them, you were never a sister.
and managers don't get to clock out.

title: dad's twin
lines: but only about the good parts.
you became the son he wanted,
on shoulders too small for the weight.
fixing things, being logical, staying strong.
reflecting only what he wanted to see.

title: mom's therapist
lines: she told you about the marriage problems
before you knew what marriage meant.
like you were qualified to hold them.
at ten, you knew which fights meant divorce threats.
at twelve, you coached her through dad's indiscretions.
now you recognize every emotional manipulation
because you’ve been trained since birth.
you can spot a guilt trip from miles away.
the therapy she needed, you became.
the childhood you needed, you never got.

title: the family mediator
lines: you learned to read the room
mom's tight smile meant perform happiness.
the bridge over their burnt bridges.
you carried messages like a wartime courier,
but who mediates for the mediator?
who notices when you’re the one

title: the translator
lines: what dad means, what mom says,
and what everyone needs to hear.
you’re subtitling everyone’s subtext in real-time.
"she didn’t mean it that way," you soothe.
means never speaking your own language.

title: the human shield
lines: between them and your siblings like armor.
absorbed dad’s bad moods so they wouldn’t.
took mom’s frustration so they could play.
every harsh word that hit you

title: the family memory keeper
lines: you carry the family history like a burden,
remembering what everyone else gets to forget.
the keeper of secrets, grudges, and patterns.
but can’t make anyone else notice.
it’s exhausting being the only one who remembers,
sometimes you wish you could forget too.

title: the achievement trophy
lines: because that would make them look bad.
they displayed you at family gatherings
like proof they did something right.

title: the practice child
lines: where they made all their mistakes.
too strict with you, too lenient with them.
too demanding of you, too forgiving of them.
you watched your siblings get the parents you needed:
"we learned from our mistakes," they say,
the practice child who taught them
by the time they got it right,

title: the anger that’s too much
lines: you absorbed their chaos without complaint.
but only because they never let it be enough

title: parentification: when kids raise kids
paras: can you remember where you were when you got the news that you were going to have a younger sibling? maybe your parents took you out to your favorite restaurant: they bought you a burger with fries on the side and a milkshake to boot. maybe you had an inkling of what they were about to tell you; chances are, though, you were just happy to be eating out, enjoying your favorite meal.
and when you finally got the news, how did you handle it?
“you’re going to be a big sister,” they told you. what they didn’t tell you was that you were also going to become the third parent.

it started slowly once your younger sibling finally arrived: mom would ask you to help out with dinner, or change the little one’s diaper. looking down at your younger sibling, soiled diaper in hand, you couldn’t conceive that you were in their place not too long ago. whether you knew it then or not, you were no longer your parents’ baby: you were their little helper.

title: instrumental parentification: being the helper
paras: you hold the diaper in your hands, at arm’s length, as far away from your nose as possible. it’s been hastily bundled up: you have no idea what you’re doing at this point. but there’s a strange sort of pride in what you’re doing, too. you feel as though you have been entrusted with the most important task in the entire world. and so, holding your breath, you dispose of the soiled bundle and wrap the baby up in a new diaper. it’s a rush job: you have no idea what you’re doing; you only know that this will make your parents proud.

this is where instrumental parentification begins. you don’t know it yet, but this is far from the last diaper you’ll have to change. it doesn’t even occur to you, then, that you were soiling diapers yourself not too long ago.

as financial worries, stress, and the heavy burden of raising a family begin to set in on your parents, you find yourself, more and more, doing all sorts of tasks around the house. most kids object to doing chores, but not you. washing the dishes and mopping the floor isn’t fun, but you don’t want to let down your parents. no, never that. after all, you’re the big sister, remember?

title: emotional parentification: developing a strong shoulder
paras: conflict occurs in every household. you don’t remember your parents fighting when you were still an only child. back then, you likely had an entire room to yourself and plenty of things to do that kept your head in the clouds. but when your younger sibling showed up, you began to notice it more and more.

your parents just seemed more tired in those days, more vulnerable. they would sigh heavily when they got home from work, collapsing on the couch at the first chance they got. and there was something… pained about them. you didn’t have the words for it then: you just knew that they needed help. nowadays, being all grown up, you probably know exactly what they were feeling at the time. back then, however, you could only listen when your parents complained to you about their jobs, about their friends, and, unthinkably, about each other.

this was the beginning of emotional parentification. as time went on, your parents came to rely on you more and more for emotional support, and you found yourself playing therapist at a young age. their overreliance on you for support conditioned you: it made you hyperaware of people’s thoughts and emotions at any given time. you could (and probably still can, to this day) sense when a fight was about to break out, or when one parent had inadvertently upset the other. you developed a keen emotional intelligence at an age when the emotional range of most kids was comparable to that of a teaspoon.

title: emotional labor at a young age
paras: of course, the effects of emotional parentification don’t stop there. more than just becoming extremely aware of the emotions of others, at some point, you probably also learned to suppress your own. some people call this “emotional maturity”: you are confronted with emotionally straining or demanding situations, but rather than expressing the sadness or anger you may feel, you bury it away, you know, in the way that adults are so fond of. except you weren’t an adult then; you were a kid who didn’t feel as though she was allowed to express her own feelings for fear of upsetting the status quo. and maybe it worked: maybe all those years of bottling your emotions away kept certain conflicts from escalating, or, at the very least, mitigated their effects.

but these days? these days, you have to bear the consequences of emotional parentification. stress, anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem: the idea that your feelings aren’t worth the trouble: these are all symptoms of being a big sister.

title: growing up too fast
paras: “the last time i saw you, you were this big,” says a distant relative of yours. “i’m going to have to put a brick on your head: you’re growing up too fast!” and they couldn’t have been more right.

one of the great tragedies of being a big sister is missing out on a childhood that you never even got to say goodbye to. one day you’re playing outside without a care in the world; the next day, you’re changing diapers, washing dishes, or mediating an argument between your parents.

the shift is sudden, abrupt, leaving you no chance at all to mourn the fun you’re missing out on. at the time, it probably felt like the most natural thing in the world: no one ever told you that big sisters deserve to have a childhood, too, and so you fell into your duties without argument. “i guess this is just what it’s supposed to be like,” you tell yourself.
you left your favorite plushy outside and didn’t even realize until later.

title: cultural expectations
paras: look, it’s no secret that the “responsible, mature eldest daughter” is kind of a stereotype, perpetuated by more people than just your immediate family. again, there is a certain pride in living up to this image of the perfectly put-together woman who has everything under control at all times, thank you very much. but it’s important to recognize that that’s all it is: an idea, a fantasy.

the exact role of eldest daughters, and women in general, varies from culture to culture, but you’re probably intimately familiar with most of the broad assumptions people make about us. and while there is a real, genuine power in being strong and independent, society makes it so that it’s not just your parents that you need to “answer” to: it’s everyone.
and it’s absolutely, utterly exhausting.

title: birth order shaping identity
paras: think back to the time when you first heard that you were going to have a younger sibling. maybe you were excited at the idea of having a baby around, someone who would eventually grow up to become your best-est friend in the world, or maybe you were dismayed at the fact that you were now going to have to share a space with someone else.
both feelings are completely valid and completely normal. what you probably didn’t realize then was that this new life that would be entering your home would actually shape your identity.

everything we’ve talked about so far isn’t just a feeling. people have been writing about birth order for over a hundred years. now, we won’t get into the specifics, but see if any of these traits sound at all familiar:
● high-achieving (possibly even over-achieving)
● structured
● responsible
● mature
● nurturing
● strict
● cautious

sound like someone you know? you, perhaps? that’s right: being a big sister didn’t just come with a brand new title and set of responsibilities: it came with an entire shift in your personality, too. contrast these adjectives with the ones you may use to describe your younger sibling(s): immature, irresponsible, outgoing, free-spirited, etc. there’s nothing wrong with being any of these things, but it’s a privilege that was never afforded to you.

title: silent family expectations
paras: the funny thing about eldest daughter syndrome and the challenges that come with it is that they’re often easy to recognize in hindsight. when you first stepped into the shoes of the older sibling, it’s unlikely that your parents sat you down and clearly laid out your new responsibilities and the expectations they had of you.
after a while, though, they didn’t need to: you felt it clearly in the disapproving head-shakes when you dared to indulge your inner child.

one of the great childhood killers is the idea that older siblings should set the example for their younger siblings to follow. before they arrived, you could act out, be punished for it, and have that be the end of it. as soon as they arrived, however, the consequences of any slip-ups or mistakes somehow felt more dire. maybe your parents never told you directly that the way you acted would influence your siblings, but it was something you were likely keenly aware of nonetheless.

title: guilt for wanting freedom
paras: it wasn’t enough that you had to be the big sister: you had to be your siblings’ main role model, too. but what child can be expected to be on their best behavior at all times?

being the big sister forces you to become a master of many vocations: cleaner, nanny, babysitter, cook, therapist. maybe you enjoyed the challenge, and maybe you appreciate the skills you were able to develop at such a young age. consider this, though: it takes at least four years to earn a degree in one subject. the average adult isn’t expected to wear that many hats. so why did you have to?

at some point, maybe, the pressure began to build up to a breaking point. days, weeks, months, years of being there for everyone at any given moment begin to take their toll, and you find yourself yearning for some sort of relief. “i just want a break,” you say out loud one day… and immediately regret it. feeling as though you’ve just uttered some unspeakable blasphemy, you tell yourself that breaks are for kids. what you don’t realize then, and maybe even now, is that your responsibilities never end, and only continue to mount.

title: the truth about parents
paras: nobody is perfect, not even your parents. circumstances and family dynamics are completely different for everybody, and despite the burdens you may bear as the eldest daughter, none of this is to say that your parents messed up in raising you.
with that said, however, it’s important to recognize the truth about parents, and that is: it was never your responsibility to be the role model: it was theirs.

all the responsibilities you shouldered, all the mediating you did, the diapers you changed, none of these things should have been your cross to bear. of course, there will always be some responsibility in being the eldest daughter, but rather than becoming a role model for your younger siblings, your parents should have encouraged something far more important: being there for your siblings.

the point is this: the standards you may hold yourself to now are not your fault. the weight of all those responsibilities is heavy, and it’s easy to be crushed by it all from time to time. understanding where it all comes from and, most importantly, identifying it by giving it a name are the first steps in learning to put it down. so, let’s just call it what it is:
eldest daughter syndrome.

title: anger as protection
paras: you don’t think of yourself as an angry person. in fact, most people would agree that you’re perfectly pleasant, polite, always remembering your “please’s” and “thank you’s”. every day, when you come into work, you give it your all and get along well with your coworkers. “there’s no way that someone can have it so under control all the time, right?” they wonder.
you’re remarkably good at putting on a brave face: even when, deep down, all you want to do is scream.

you probably weren’t a particularly angry child, at least not for the first few years of your life. but when your younger siblings came into the picture and you were forced to be responsible for their well-being, something changed in you. you found yourself constantly frustrated with their behavior. “why won’t you just eat your vegetables? is it so hard to clean up after yourself?” and so on, and so forth until it all just… came out one day.

maybe you shouted, maybe you cried, but after putting up with everybody else’s problems at such a young age, you had had enough. you had no other option, nobody you could rely on for comfort, nowhere to go but the home you grew up in. anger, it seemed, was about the only thing that seemed at all relieving. but it came with a cost, too.

title: the anger-guilt cycle
paras: you and your younger sister were at home alone one day after school. your parents would be home in an hour or two, and they entrusted you with ensuring that the house wasn’t burned down. that meant cleaning the place up, doing the dishes… and making sure your sister was okay.

she was playing near a table, atop which sat one of your mother’s cherished vases. you saw her bump it once and immediately told her not to play there, for fear of the vase shattering. you got on with the dishes, humming along to a song in your head when… crash.
you knew exactly what it was without even having to see it.

coming back into the room, your eyes dart from your sister to the shattered remains of the vase, back to your sister. she looks totally… clueless about what she’s done: so you make sure that she knows, as loud and as angrily as possible.
your face is flushed, your throat hurts a little from shouting, your hands have clenched into balls: you know that you’re perfectly justified in your anger. and yet…
you simply can’t stand the sight of your baby sister crying.
wiping away the tears of your own that have just begun to well up in your eyes, you go over to her, wrapping her up in your arms, suddenly completely ashamed of having been so angry.
this is hardly the last time in your life that this happens.

title: perfectionism-as-survival
paras: as the eldest sibling, you were always expected to be perfect in everything you did. you set the standard, remember? school work, chores, it didn’t matter: everything you did had to be absolutely, indisputably golden.

you can probably still recall the sheer terror of report card day at school. it didn’t matter how much you studied and how much work you put in: there was always the chance of receiving a bad grade. you would open your report card with trembling hands, then rapidly scan it for anything that wasn’t an “a”.
and there it was, mocking you: a “b”.

this seemed like the end of the world at the time. your parents would shrug it off and tell you to just work a bit harder next time. didn’t they know? you had already given it all the effort you could muster. and so, knowing that 100% wasn’t enough, you gave it 110% next time. and the next time, and the next time after that. you feel as though the world would end if you ever allowed yourself to put in even 90% of effort into anything you did, even something as small as a grocery list (color-coordinated, of course). but wouldn’t it be nice if instead of battening down the hatches, manning the wheel, and swinging the jib all by yourself, all the damn time, you simply cruised?

title: “old souls”: being too mature too soon
paras: one thing you can bet that every eldest daughter has heard at some point in their life is that she’s “so mature for her age”. thanks, but we didn’t really have a choice.

you couldn’t say where this maturity came from. it’s another one of those things that just sort of happened overnight, around the time your younger siblings were born. the more you took care of them and shouldered more responsibilities around the house, the less childlike you became. school holidays didn’t bring with them a sense of unbridled joy anymore: it just meant more time at home, doing chores and looking after your siblings. playing outside wasn’t so appealing when you knew that there were dishes to be washed or clothes to be folded. and so, your eyes lost a bit of their sparkle. when older people would meet you, they would call you an “old soul” simply because you didn’t run around and play like other kids your age. you may have even taken this as a compliment at the time, but it’s really just another tragedy.

nowadays, when your friends want to go out for a drink or hit the club, you’re more inclined to stay at home and get things done around the house. you’re not an “old soul” anymore: you just feel like a party-pooper.

title: hyper-vigilance
paras: you can remember going to the grocery store with your parents when you were still an only child. you would run from aisle to aisle looking for toys and candy, blissfully unaware of the strangers around you. as soon as you became a big sister, however, things changed. now it was your sibling running around, and you chasing after them to make sure they were safe. suddenly, all those strangers who were so benign before seemed much more… sinister.

not much has changed since then. you’re constantly on edge wherever you go, always alert and ready to protect yourself and your loved ones from danger. it’s exhausting, yes, but you tell yourself that hyper-vigilance is at least better than ignorance.

of course, your younger siblings aren’t like this. they’ll go home with random people they meet at the club, attend a house party in a dangerous neighborhood, or take a drink from the “friendly, charming man” at the bar. it must be nice to be able to go through life without any worry whatsoever, but that’s not a luxury you can afford.

title: silencing your own needs
paras: of course, even when considering everything you’ve read so far, most of this probably isn’t new to you. far from it: as the eldest daughter, you’ve likely always held yourself to a high standard, which means you’re likely also very self-aware.

at some point in your young life, it probably occurred to you that you were always working too hard. you would get home exhausted after a long day at school, only to be immediately thrust back into your chores. at night, you would study while everyone else watched tv. it was only on the weekends when you could finally have some time to yourself… if not for the fact that your siblings still needed looking after. you would tell yourself that you just needed more time in the day to get everything done and still do something for yourself.
what you really needed, though, was a break.

you’ve needed a break your whole life. you’ve needed a chance to indulge in your own interests for a change, to take care of yourself instead of looking after others all the time. but there’s simply too much that needs to get done. you’d love to spend an hour or two at the spa or in the salon, but you don’t even have five minutes to spare.
you tell yourself that “me-time” and looking after your own needs are just two more luxuries that you simply can’t afford. at least your siblings get to have fun, right?

title: hiding emotions to protect others
paras: you know that crying isn’t a weak thing to do, but it’s not something you’ll admit to doing yourself. when you do allow yourself to shed a few tears, it’s usually in isolation, away from anyone who might witness: you don’t want to burden anyone else with your feelings.

of course, your parents never hesitated in divulging their struggles to you when you were a kid. you were always there to listen or come between them when things got heated. you comforted your younger siblings when they were upset, wiping their tears and giving them tissues. you probably can’t think of a single time in your life when someone did the same for you.

you can’t blame anyone, though. they don’t know what you go through because you make an effort to hide your emotions in order to protect them. after all, why should anyone else have to shoulder your burdens for you?
you cry for a minute or two in your car outside the office on some mornings, then redo your makeup before going inside. no one will ever know.

title: you can do it yourself
paras: being the eldest daughter means being responsible for everyone else in the house, including your parents. you’re the one who makes sure that your siblings do their homework, who settles arguments between them, and who keeps your parents in the loop. they may have been totally clueless about what went on in the lives of your siblings if not for you.

it’s difficult to not develop some sort of complex from this. having to wear so many hats at such a young age matures you quickly, but also puts you in a uniquely powerful position. you may not admit it, but you know, deep down, just how integral you are to the lives of your family. without you, they would surely have gone mad by now!

unfortunately, this power is something of a double-edged sword. you’re able to juggle plenty of tasks and responsibilities all at once, but even you are just a human. it’s a tough thing to admit that sometimes you need a little help. you would never ask your younger siblings for anything when you were a kid: what could they possibly do to help? your parents were a no-go, too: they had their own problems to deal with!
even now, it’s difficult for you to ask for help because you know that with all the time in the world, you would never need to ask anyone for anything.

title: self-worth tied to success
paras: the worst thing you can say to a child, not just eldest daughters, is those four dreadful words: “i’m disappointed in you”.

these words sting a little more for eldest daughters, though. growing up as the beacon of responsibility and maturity of the household meant that you were also always trying to live up to others’ expectations of you. it was like being placed at the precipice of a cliff: you would clutch on for dear life, knowing that letting go meant certain doom.

when you did slip up (not that it happened often, mind you), it felt as though you had failed some unspoken moral test. you’d leave one dish unwashed and feel as though you’d committed the most grievous sin known to man, or come home with a dreaded “b” on your report card and want to lock yourself up for the school holidays because you didn’t deserve to have fun.

title: the eternal outsider
paras: perhaps the most tragic aspect of all of this is that you may feel as though you don’t belong anywhere. people value you because of what you can do for them, not because of who you are as a person. as soon as you stop being “useful”, you stop being likeable, too…
at least, that’s what you may think.

it can be difficult to find people who relate to these very specific trials and experiences. growing up, you were always the responsible one, and not much has changed now. you’re the designated driver at parties, and the one others turn to when they need a shoulder to cry on.
but that’s exactly what these essays hope to prove: that you’re not alone.

title: hyper-independence
paras: when was the last time you asked for help? it’s probably been a few years by now since it ever occurred to you that you weren’t alone. if you’re like us and many other eldest daughters, you probably haven’t been able to rely on someone since before your siblings arrived.
independence could hardly be considered a negative trait. when it comes down to it, it’s good to be able to rely on yourself, especially if you’re still finding your way around adult life.

hyper-independence, on the other hand, is an entirely different sort of self-reliance. it’s sort of like going to an ikea factory and building all the parts yourself, then assembling them without a manual or guide.

of course, no one can blame you for being this way. as far back as you can remember, you’ve always had to do everything yourself. mom and dad were always too busy raising your siblings to help you with your homework or school project. they probably figured you’d be okay: after all, you were always so mature for your age, remember?
but life isn’t a school project. you’re tough, but sometimes life is tougher. and on your worst days, you feel like a little girl again, stuck with a math problem you haven’t got an answer to.

title: fear of asking for help
paras: hyper-independence is itself a symptom of neglect, even if that neglect was unintentional. that’s the burden that eldest daughters bear, being the one who nobody thinks of because “she’s always been able to think for herself”. but hyper-independence also comes with its own share of symptoms.

perhaps the most notable of these is the fear of asking for help. it’s something you can’t explain. you recognize the value of not facing your problems alone, but on some fundamental level, it feels wrong to ask someone for help.

you can remember being a kid and asking your dad for help with a project, but he was always too tired from work to offer you any meaningful aid. ditto for mom, who was always juggling the needs of your other siblings before your own. watching them struggle with their own responsibilities and priorities left you feeling sorry that you ever asked.

the older you got, the more self-reliant you became, to the point where the words “please could you…” were no longer part of your vocabulary. even now, you can hardly wrap your mouth around them. you’d rather bite the bullet yourself and deal with your problems alone, even if it costs you your emotional well-being. at least you can’t say no to yourself.

title: people-pleasing in relationships
paras: self-worth is a funny thing. as a strong, independent, and capable woman, you’re typically full of confidence. after all, you’ve managed to get this far in life without anybody’s help, so why shouldn’t you be?

but here’s the thing: you only feel good about yourself when you’re serving others. it’s likely been this way for as long as you can remember. you’d clean the house all day and wash the dishes and toil away just to hear your parents say “thank you”. mom would call you her little helper and you’d wear the badge with pride. in relationships, you want nothing more than to make your partner happy regardless of the potential cost to your own wellbeing. but people, all people, will slip up every now and then, even you. and as soon as you disappoint someone, your confidence goes into freefall. you miss a deadline at work and it feels like you’re a little girl again being told to go to her room. you can be full of smiles all day, but as soon as you feel like you’ve disappointed someone, the tears come easily.

no one can blame you for being this way: throughout your life, you’ve always been praised for what you do, not who you are. you’re not a person; you’re the big sister; you’re momma’s little helper; you’re the responsible one; you’re the old soul.
you were told this all your life and eventually you came to define yourself by these titles, too. but you need to know that you’re more than just what you can do for other people.
